extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers of science, and students learning the scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing or producing scientific theories/ explanations: how to discover laws, deduce consequences, and verify them against observation; includes modes of explanation (resolution into causes, intermediate links, subsumption) and criteria for generality and reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive Method components (Induction, Ratiocination, Verification)
rubrics_metrics.description: To the Deductive Method, thus characterized in its three constituent parts, Induction, Ratiocination, and Verification, the human mind is indebted for its most conspicuous triumphs in the investigation of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any deductive scientific work should include: (1) induction (ascertaining empirical generalities), (2) ratiocination/deduction (deriving consequences from laws), and (3) verification (comparing deduced conclusions with observation). Without verification, deductive results are little more than conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification: compare deductions with direct observation
rubrics_metrics.description: To warrant reliance on the general conclusions arrived at by deduction, these conclusions must be found, on careful comparison, to accord with the results of direct observation wherever it can be had.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a theory, verify its deduced predictions against observed instances. Use existing experience to confirm theory and only then safely apply it to new cases. If observations contradict predictions, the theory must explain the discrepancy or be regarded as imperfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain discrepancies: identify frustrating causes
rubrics_metrics.description: If our deductions have led to the conclusion that from a particular combination of causes a given effect would result, then in all known cases where that combination can be shown to have existed, and where the effect has not followed, we must be able to show (or at least to make a probable surmise) what frustrated it: if we can not, the theory is imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sound theory should account for apparent counterexamples by identifying additional conditions or interfering factors. Mere denial of counterexamples without plausible explanation undermines reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of verification requires cases of comparable complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Nor is the verification complete, unless some of the cases in which the theory is borne out by the observed result are of at least equal complexity with any other cases in which its application could be called for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify a theory not only in simplified circumstances but also in instances as complex as intended applications; success only in oversimplified tests is insufficient to establish practical reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best verification: theory deduces known empirical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: If direct observation and collation of instances have furnished us with any empirical laws of the effect... the most effectual verification of which the theory could be susceptible, would be, that it led deductively to those empirical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A theory that deductively yields previously observed empirical regularities (e.g., Newton's theory leading to Kepler's laws) gains strong confirmation. When evaluating, check whether the theory explains existing empirical laws, not merely isolated facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect comprehensive empirical laws (Method of Agreement) and accurate descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important that as many as possible of the empirical laws of the phenomena should be ascertained, by a comparison of instances, conformably to the Method of Agreement: as well as... that the phenomena themselves should be described, in the most comprehensive as well as accurate manner possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical groundwork is essential: gather many instances, compare them (Method of Agreement), and describe phenomena precisely to facilitate verification and theory formulation. Poorly described data weakens verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use complex cases as additional verification (even if not useful for discovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex instances which would have been of no use for the discovery of the simple laws... nevertheless, when they have served to verify the analysis, become additional evidence of the laws themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that complex, real-world cases can confirm a law found under simpler conditions and may reveal omitted circumstances. Include such cases in evaluation to strengthen confidence in a theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution into separate laws of causes plus collocations
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of the complex effect is explained, by being resolved into the separate laws of the causes which contribute to it... it is resolved into the laws of the separate causes, together with the fact of their co-existence (collocations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining or assessing a complex-effect law, identify each contributing causal law and the required co-existence/arrangement of causes. Evaluations must consider both elemental causal laws and whether the necessary collocations obtain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate-link explanation (A→B→C): resolve remote sequences into proximate links
rubrics_metrics.description: A seemed the cause of C, but it subsequently appeared that A was only the cause of B, and that it is B which was the cause of C... the sequence... is resolved into two other laws—the law that A produces B and the law that B produces C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether an apparent direct cause–effect relation masks intermediate processes. Demonstrating intermediary links often produces more general and reliable laws; when reviewing, look for missing intermediate mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsumption: generalize partial laws under a more general law
rubrics_metrics.description: The third mode is the subsumption... the gathering up of several laws into one more general law which includes them all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether separate partial laws across different classes of cases can legitimately be combined and explained by a single more general law. Subsumption requires showing commonalities and eliminating special circumstances (e.g., unifying terrestrial and celestial gravity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality and reliability: laws resolved into more general laws are more certain
rubrics_metrics.description: In all these three processes, laws are... resolved into laws more general than themselves... they are, in fact, proved not to be themselves laws of nature, the character of which is to be universally true, but results of laws of nature, which may be only true conditionally, and for the most part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer explanations that reduce conditional/complex laws to more general, simpler laws. Such reduction tends to increase the range and certainty of claims. When appraising theory, favor parsimonious generalizations that subsume many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex laws are less general and more liable to failure than simpler causal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of a complex effect must be less general than the laws of the causes which conspire to produce it... The complex law is liable to be oftener unfulfilled than any one of the simpler laws of which it is the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat compound predictions cautiously: they inherit failure modes of all constituent causes and additional contingencies. Evaluation should test components separately and in combination; vulnerability of any component undermines the complex law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportional/collocation sensitivity: small changes can change qualitative outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: The same causes, acting according to the same laws, and differing only in the proportions in which they are combined, often produce effects which differ not merely in quantity, but in kind... the combination... gives rise to an elliptical motion; but if the ratio... were slightly altered... the motion produced would be... a parabola, or an hyperbola.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate robustness: check how sensitive predicted phenomena are to variations in proportions or arrangement of causes. Small quantitative changes may yield qualitatively different behaviors, so robustness analysis is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation = deriving a partial law from more general laws + collocations (not giving ultimate 'why')
rubrics_metrics.description: In science, explaining any phenomenon mean(s)... pointing out... some more general phenomenon, of which it is a partial exemplification; or some laws of causation which produce it by their joint or successive action... The word explanation... does nothing to render the general course of nature other than mysterious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming to 'explain' a law, be precise: show the derivation from more general laws plus required collocations. Avoid overstating that explanation uncovers ultimate causes; it replaces one level of generality with another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming very general laws requires diverse, independent sets of observations
rubrics_metrics.description: To arrive by correct induction at laws which hold under such an immense variety of circumstances... requires for the most part many distinct sets of experiments or observations, conducted at different times and by different people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess evidence breadth: general laws should be supported by independent observations across different contexts, times, and observers. Single-source or narrowly scoped data cannot establish universally-applicable laws.
